issues.legal_issue: A supervisory court exceeds its limited jurisdiction when it reassesses the merits of a proposed pleading amendment to overturn the trial court’s decision allowing it.
material_facts: The trial court allowed an application to amend a written statement.
The High Court set aside that order after considering whether the proposed defence was legally tenable on its merits.
The proposed defence elaborated on a joint-family-property defence already pleaded in the written statement.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s order was unsustainable because it went beyond the limits of supervisory jurisdiction; the trial court’s order allowing the amendment was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 227 of the Constitution, supervisory jurisdiction is confined to determining whether the inferior court or tribunal acted within its jurisdiction; the High Court does not act as an appellate court or reassess the merits of the evidence or proposed case. The Court relied on Sadhna Lodh v National Insurance Company, (2003) 3 SCC 524.

predicates.appeal_challenges_supervisory_interferen: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a supervisory court’s intervention in a trial court’s order.
predicates.trial_court_allowed_pleading_amendment: The trial court allowed a party to amend a pleading.
predicates.supervisory_court_assessed_amendment_mer: The supervisory court assessed the merits of the case proposed by the amendment when intervening.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges supervisory intervention in an order allowing a pleading amendment and the intervention rests on assessing the amendment’s merits, the supervisory court cannot set aside that order on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment to a written statement may be allowed when it elaborates an existing defence rather than withdrawing an admission and causes no prejudice to the opposing party.
material_facts: The original written statement already alleged that the property was joint-family property and described a joint-family arrangement.
The proposed amendment added detail about the property’s inheritance and asserted coparcenary rights.
After the plaint was amended, the defendant had filed a written statement responding to the amended plaint.
The Court found that the proposed amendment elaborated the existing defence, would not withdraw an admission, and would cause no prejudice to the plaintiff.
issues.conclusion: The amendment of the written statement was properly allowed, and the trial court’s order allowing it was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs amendment of pleadings. Whether an amendment should be allowed does not depend on whether the proposed case will ultimately succeed at trial. An amendment elaborating an existing defence does not amount to withdrawal of an admission, and the Court noted that this amendment would cause no prejudice to the plaintiff.

predicates.civil_suit_involves_pleading_amendment: The proceeding is a civil suit in which a party seeks to amend a pleading.
predicates.proposed_written_statement_elaborates_ex: The proposed written-statement amendment adds detail to a defence already pleaded rather than replacing it with a new defence.
predicates.amendment_causes_no_prejudice: Allowing the amendment would not prejudice the opposing party.

issues.definition: In a civil suit, a written-statement amendment that elaborates an existing defence and causes no prejudice may be allowed.
